av3zdxYvCp8.tx: For over four decades, Walter Cavanagh held a truly credit-worthy record: the most credit cards held by one person. What began as a bet between friends led him to open over 1,400 cards, ranging from traditional bank-issued to those from airlines, gas stations, and even ice cream shops. Most people have far fewer credit cards. While useful for secure purchasing, handling emergencies, and building credit scores, credit cards can make it difficult to avoid overspending. Globally, the outstanding credit card debt exceeds trillions of dollars. And this is no accident. Credit card companies intentionally design these systems to encourage spending and lock you into a cycle of interest and fees. So, how can you avoid their most common traps? It starts with card selection. Lenders often aggressively advertise perks like cash back, travel miles, and discounts. But these offers only seem generous. In reality, only a small portion of cardholders actually benefit— those who pay off their entire balance every month. But according to one survey, 46% of American cardholders carry a revolving balance. For these users, the cost of interest and fees almost always exceeds the value of rewards. If you think you may fall into this category, financial experts recommend getting a card with the lowest annual percentage rate, or APR. This number is essentially the cost of borrowing money from the credit card company. You pay that cost through interest charges, which kick in as soon as you carry any balance past a statement due date. While APRs are listed as yearly rates, for most cards, interest accrues daily. For example, a card with a 35% APR charges about 0.095% interest per day. So a revolving balance of $1,000 would accumulate approximately $29 in interest over a month. Meanwhile, a card with a lower APR, say 18%, would charge about $15 in interest during the same period. This difference can add up over time. If you were to make a $50 monthly payment towards that $1,000 balance, the card with the higher APR would take an extra $325 and an extra seven months to pay off. And interest fees can be even more complicated. If you carry a balance and actively use a card, new purchases start accruing interest immediately, even if you pay off those purchases before the statement date. In other words, once you start to carry a balance, it’s much more difficult to avoid interest charges going forward. And even after a bill is fully paid, you might still get one more charge, something called residual interest, for the days between your statement and payment date. Low APR cards are the best option for minimizing these interest charges; however, be wary of cards that offer exceptionally low APR for an introductory period. These flashy offers can mask things like complicated fee structures, steep late charges, and high default APRs that kick in once the introductory period ends. While many countries require companies to disclose these conditions, they're often buried in the fine print. Payment structures can also be confusing. For example, many people mistake the minimum payment as the standard or even recommended amount to pay. In reality, it typically only covers interest, fees, and a small percentage of the balance. As a result, sticking to just the minimum payment can make even a low balance of $1,000 take over 18 years to pay off. Paying the full card balance each month is the best way to avoid fees and actually benefit from rewards. But it's not always possible. So what should you do if you find yourself in credit card debt? The first step is to assess your finances and create a repayment plan. If the debt is on a high APR card, transferring your balance to a lower APR card may help. Just be sure to check for balance transfer fees. If you’re juggling debt on multiple cards, it may be tempting to pay off the lowest balance first. However, the most financially efficient strategy will always be to put any extra money towards the card with the highest APR, regardless of balance. The key is to chip away one card at a time— just don’t be like Walter and open a thousand more in the meantime.

Unfortunately, this era is also associated with rigid gender roles, deep class divisions, and the subjugation of colonized peoples— all reinforced by Queen Victoria's so-called virtues. In her defense, Your Honor, Victoria came to the throne at the tender age of 18 and faced immediate pressure to restore public faith in the crown. The previous two kings had been drinkers, womanizers, and gamblers. Meanwhile, Victoria was expected to serve as the country's moral compass during the dizzying changes brought by industrialization. Well, she certainly got her chance. Her reign coincided with the birth of mass media, giving her the power to exert immense cultural influence. In newspapers, she appeared as the perfect wife to her beloved Prince Albert. Press images of her pure white wedding dress started a fashion trend that continues to this day. And front pages featuring their family’s idyllic Christmas celebrations set a new standard for middle class society. Specifically a standard that shamed any family who couldn’t afford a picture-perfect holiday. But I'd like to suggest something unexpected. Food. Food may be as essential to a strong democracy if we accept two simple ideas. First, democracy relies upon us knowing each other. Being able to talk to one another. Understanding that disagreement does not make someone an enemy. And second, food is one of our last common denominators. No matter your race, income or religion, we all have a cuisine. And those cuisines are more than just their ingredients. They're collections of stories, histories, values, memories. When we start to learn something about one another's cuisine, we often discover something deeper. We are not as different from each other as we think. Twelve immigrant and native-born communities came together in partnership with the Reading Terminal Market, the city and local organizations. We cooked together, ate together, talked through facilitated dialogue, almost entirely about food, over dinner with strangers we may otherwise never meet. Folks sharing recipes on how chicken is fried in their respective cultures. Trading stories about Sunday night dinner traditions with extended family. Talking about those food-centered holidays we all celebrate. Over the years, nearly 400 Philadelphians took part in four different versions, and this year, for our 250th anniversary, over 700, across seven Philly neighborhoods, are taking part in a version that has catalyzed a city-wide conversation on citizenship, at a time when that word divides more often than it unites. What I've witnessed over the years has been profound. War-weary Syrian refugees being welcomed over dinner by their new neighbors in Northeast Philly as if they'd known each other for decades. A single mother, isolated during the pandemic, sharing through a virtual dinner with strangers that this was the first human interaction she'd had in nearly a year since the pandemic began beyond her immediate family. And a 12-year-old boy, standing unsolicited in a room full of adults to simply state: if more people took the time to learn about each other, the world would be a richer place. bw5tzcoEG88.tx: If you could wave a magic wand, what’s the one idea you’d most love to spread to other people’s minds? Through the power of language— carefully used— we can do just that. But what’s the most direct way of gifting an idea to an audience? Simply show it. Incorporating visuals can make a talk more powerful and convincing. Assuming you have your throughline and talk content, it's time to get this show on the road. In the 21st century, we can add to the spoken word with many technologies— pictures, illustrations, graphs, charts, animation, video, audio, and data. All can help explain your idea and make your talk visually interesting. But first, ask yourself whether you actually need visuals. At least a third of TED’s most-viewed talks don’t use slides at all. Slides move attention away from the speaker. If your talk relies on personal connection, humor, or stories, you may be better off speaking directly to the audience. For every speaker, the rule is simple: having no slides is better than having bad slides. But many talks benefit from strong visuals. Sometimes, the visuals make the talk a success. Key components of strong visuals fall into three categories: revelation, explanatory power, and aesthetic appeal. Revelation: The most obvious reason to use visuals is to show something hard to describe. Edith Widder was part of the team that first captured the giant squid on video. Her talk was built around that moment of revelation. When the creature appeared on screen, the audience nearly jumped out of its skin. Revelation doesn't have to be dramatic. Explain any background, prime the audience, and then let the visuals do their work. Run them full screen without adding anything. Explanatory power: Words and images often explain best together. Much of our world is imagined visually. To explain something new, showing and telling often works best. But the visual must fit the spoken message. Complicated slides can distract an audience. Limit each slide to one core idea. Multiple streams of information require mental energy to process. A speaker must direct attention so slides support, For graphs and charts, highlight the relevant parts. If comparing February and October rainfall, use colors to show the months. Don't cram everything onto one slide. Headlines with long bullet points often lose attention— turn bullets into separate slides, reduce phrases, or replace them with images. Even simple slides may steal your thunder. Instead of “A black hole is an object so massive that no light can escape,” try: “How black is a black hole?” Then deliver the information through speech; The slide teases curiosity and makes words more compelling. Visuals shouldn't communicate words your mouth can easily say. Use them to share what speech can’t: photographs, video, animation, or data. Screens can explain instantly what might take hours to describe. Aesthetic appeal: Nice-looking slides add power. Visually appealing slides can amplify a talk's impact. Hans Rosling is a TED speaker who excelled at this. “Here we go. Can you see there? It’s China. They’re moving — better health. They are improving. There, all the green Latin American countries. They are moving towards smaller families.” Not everyone can be a Hans Rosling, but every speaker can ask: are visuals essential for explaining my idea? And how can I combine them effectively with words? Once you plan your visuals, revisit your words and figure out how to turn them into a rewarding presentation. All these lessons should put you on your way to delivering a powerful talk— one that inspires, delights, and may even change the world.

BSdEiOYvKpE.tx: In 1930, as the Great Depression ravaged the United States, President Herbert Hoover made a bold economic decision. With the goal of supporting American farmers and manufacturers, he approved a sweeping 20% tax on all imported agricultural and industrial goods. He believed making foreign goods more expensive would encourage consumers to buy domestic, thus funneling cash into American businesses and creating more jobs. But Hoover's plan completely backfired. Other countries retaliated by taxing American goods, leading exports to fall and global trade to decline. In the end, this policy led American prices to spike and caused even more unemployment. These disastrous outcomes of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act were no surprise to the over 1,000 economists who publicly condemned the bill. But this wouldn’t be the last time a world leader was shocked by a tariff's consequences. So, what exactly is a tariff? A tariff is a tax an importer pays to bring foreign goods into a country. For example, if they import $1,000 worth of goods at a 10% tariff rate, they'll pay $100 to the government in addition to $1,000 to the seller. Foreign exporters could respond to a tariff by reducing their product’s price to keep an importer’s business. But if they don’t, importers bear this cost and then increase their prices so consumers will make up the difference. This may sound straightforward, but enacting a tariff kicks off a complicated economic chain reaction. So to keep things simple, let's look at some examples from just one country to explore some of the factors that make a tariff’s outcomes tricky to predict. H4KMQuyxH_Y.tx: Very tasteful art! Oh, you hate it? You are not alone! One in four people with a tattoo regret it, 25 million people in the US. Getting ink carved into your body permanently has exploded in popularity in the last few decades, especially among Millennials. Often their tattoos were about a current cultural thing, a moment in their life, following a trend, expressing individuality or about feeling like being part of something greater. This is all fine and good but as people age they often stop identifying with what their younger versions wanted on their skin forever. Or sometimes their tattoos simply just look ugly or have aged badly. And so today laser tattoo removal is booming, being as normalized as dentist appointments. Which is wild since lasering a tattoo away is one of the most metal things you can do to your body. A high tech procedure that is extremely painful and makes your skin explode from the inside. How does it work? We explained what a tattoo is in detail before, but in a nutshell: From the perspective of your cells your tattoo is a mountain range of colourful boulders, from small to building-sized. Injected deep into your dermis by violently ripping huge wounds with gigantic needles. Your body is trying hard to destroy the tattoo, but the ink particles are way too large to be transported away and your immune cells can’t eat them. So they do the next best thing: Keeping the ink trapped in a prison of flesh. This is why tattoos remain forever, millions of your cells give their lives to keep the ink in place – when they die new ones take their place. DbEZmLoGDbk.tx: Losing a loved one can be one of the most traumatic experiences of a person’s life. Grief brings on a whole host of strong emotions that impact both our mental and physical health. But is it possible for these powerful feelings to endanger your life? In other words, can you actually die from a broken heart? One of the most widely documented medical phenomena addressing this question is the widowhood effect. Studies of elderly couples have found that a person’s risk of dying can increase by up to 90% over the three months following their spouse’s death, leading a significant number of couples to pass away months, weeks, or even days apart. There are a lot of theories explaining this effect. One study found that severe grief and depression were associated with higher levels of inflammatory proteins in the blood, potentially impairing the immune system. And depression, combined with the loss of a supporting partner, can make it hard for a person to keep up with their daily health needs. Similarly, chronic stress can alter hormone levels, impair digestion, and dysregulate the immune system. But while all these factors can reduce life expectancy, there’s another condition where powerful emotions can directly endanger someone’s life: takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Also known as stress cardiomyopathy, or “broken heart syndrome,” this was originally labeled by Japanese doctors in 1990, who named the condition after the Japanese word for an octopus trap. In takotsubo cardiomyopathy, the left ventricle— one of the heart’s four chambers— pools with blood and balloons outward, giving it a distinctively takotsubo-like shape.
